exerciseDefaults.gradingInstructions: Award points for correctness and a relevant example.

exerciseRevision.exampleSolution: Use a FIFO queue, mark each vertex when enqueued, and set its distance to the parent distance plus one. BFS visits distance layers in order. DFS can first discover a longer path. Time is O(V+E); auxiliary space is O(V).
exerciseRevision.problemStatement: Given an unweighted graph and a source vertex, implement breadth-first search to compute shortest path distances. Explain why a depth-first traversal cannot guarantee shortest distances and analyze the time and space complexity.
exerciseRevision.title: Shortest paths in unweighted graphs

lecture.description: A stable lecture used for text-unit maintenance.

textUnit.content: Variables have lexical scopes and store program state. Conditional statements select branches using Boolean predicates. Loops repeat updates until a condition becomes false; an invariant describes the state that remains true after every iteration. Trace a running-sum loop and explain initialization, preservation, and termination.
textUnit.name: Algorithms maintenance

lecture.title: Algorithms maintenance lecture

lectureRevision: Graphs model networks using vertices and edges. Breadth-first search computes shortest distances in an unweighted graph by visiting distance layers in FIFO order. Dijkstra uses a priority queue to handle nonnegative weighted edges. Compare their invariants, complexity, and applicability; explain why negative edges invalidate the usual Dijkstra proof.

topics.description: Use state, branching, and loops to express deterministic programs.
exercises: Scope of a variable
Explain the difference between a local and a global variable.
A local binding is visible only within its defining scope; a global binding is visible according to the module or program scope.
Guard clauses
Rewrite nested conditionals as guard clauses and explain the benefit.
Return early for invalid or exceptional cases so the main path remains shallow and readable.
Loop invariant
State an invariant for a loop that sums the first n positive integers.
After each iteration, the accumulator equals the sum of all processed integers.
Boolean short circuit
Explain why short circuit evaluation can prevent a null dereference.
The second operand is evaluated only when the first operand allows it, so a null check can guard a member access.
Boundary conditions
Identify the boundary cases for a loop over an empty and a one element collection.
The empty collection performs zero iterations and the one element collection performs exactly one.
topics.title: Variables and control flow

topics.description: Design functions with clear contracts, parameters, and return values.
exercises: Function contract
Write the precondition and postcondition for a function that divides two numbers.
The divisor must be nonzero; the result multiplied by the divisor equals the dividend within the numeric model.
Pure function
Distinguish a pure function from one that mutates shared state.
A pure function has no observable side effects and returns the same result for the same inputs.
Parameter choice
Choose pass by value or a mutable reference when a function must update a caller-owned list.
Use a mutable reference when the contract requires updating the caller-owned list, and document that effect.
Cohesion
Explain why a function that validates input, writes a file, and sends email has low cohesion.
It combines unrelated responsibilities, making its contract and tests harder to isolate.
Error result
Compare returning an error result with throwing an exception for expected invalid input.
A result makes expected failure explicit at the call site; exceptions are better reserved for exceptional control flow.
topics.title: Functions and modularity

topics.description: Reason about base cases, recursive progress, and recursive cost.
exercises: Base case
Give a base case and progress argument for recursive factorial.
Factorial of zero is one, and each positive call reduces n by one until zero.
Tree traversal
Describe a recursive preorder traversal of a binary tree.
Visit the node, recursively traverse the left subtree, then recursively traverse the right subtree.
Recursive stack
Explain what happens to stack frames during a depth first recursive traversal.
Each descent adds a frame and each completed child returns to its caller before the next sibling is visited.
Memoization
Explain why memoization changes naive recursive Fibonacci from exponential to linear work.
Previously computed values are stored and reused, so each argument is evaluated once.
Termination
Show why a recursive search that does not shrink its input can fail to terminate.
Without a strictly smaller input or another decreasing measure, the base case may never be reached.
topics.title: Recursion

topics.description: Select sequence representations and reason about their operations.
exercises: Array lookup
Explain why indexed lookup in a fixed width array is constant time.
The address is computed from a base address and an index offset.
Linked insertion
Compare inserting at the head of a linked list with inserting at the middle of an array.
Head insertion changes a pointer in constant time; middle array insertion shifts later elements.
Amortized append
Explain why dynamic-array append is amortized constant time despite resizing.
Most appends are constant time and occasional linear copies are spread over the many successful appends.
Two pointers
Design a two-pointer scan to remove duplicates from a sorted array in place.
Advance a read pointer through values and write each new value at the next write position.
Representation choice
Choose an array or linked list for frequent random access and justify it.
An array provides direct indexed access, while a linked list requires traversal.
topics.title: Arrays and lists

topics.description: Represent hierarchical data and maintain tree invariants.
exercises: Binary search invariant
State the ordering invariant of a binary search tree.
Every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger than the node key, subject to duplicate policy.
Insertion shape
Insert 8, 3, and 10 into an empty binary search tree.
8 is the root, 3 its left child, and 10 its right child.
Balanced height
Explain why balancing a search tree improves lookup in the worst case.
Balancing keeps height logarithmic instead of allowing sorted input to create a linear chain.
Heap property
Describe the max heap property and one operation that preserves it.
Each parent is at least as large as its children; sift up or down restores the property after an update.
Traversal order
Choose inorder, preorder, or postorder for deleting a tree safely.
Postorder visits children before their parent, so subtrees can be released before the node.
topics.title: Trees

topics.description: Use hashing, collision strategies, and key equality correctly.
exercises: Collision resolution
Explain separate chaining for a hash table collision.
Colliding entries are stored in a bucket-associated collection and searched within that bucket.
Load factor
Explain why a high hash table load factor can slow lookup.
More keys per bucket increase collision chains or probing distance.
Key equality
State the relationship required between equality and hash codes.
Equal keys must produce equal hash codes so they are placed in compatible buckets.
Open addressing
Compare linear probing with chaining after a collision.
Linear probing searches subsequent slots in the table; chaining stores multiple entries outside the slot.
Mutable key
Explain why mutating a key after insertion can make a map entry unreachable.
Its new hash may point to a different bucket, so lookup using the mutated key no longer finds the stored slot.
topics.title: Hash maps

topics.description: Choose algorithms and derive their time and space costs.
exercises: Binary search invariant
Explain the invariant maintained by binary search on a sorted array.
If the target exists, it remains inside the current search interval.
Merge sort complexity
Derive the asymptotic runtime of merge sort.
There are logarithmically many levels and linear merge work per level, giving O(n log n).
Stable sorting
Define sorting stability and describe when it matters.
Equal-key records retain input order, which matters when applying successive sort keys.
Greedy counterexample
Give a coin system where taking the largest coin first is not optimal.
For coins 1, 3, and 4 with amount 6, greedy uses 4+1+1 while 3+3 is optimal.
Search selection
Choose linear or binary search for an unsorted collection and justify it.
Linear search works without preprocessing; binary search requires sorted data and offers logarithmic lookup.
topics.title: Sorting and searching

topics.description: Model relationships and traverse directed and undirected graphs.
exercises: Sparse representation
Choose an adjacency list or matrix for a sparse graph.
An adjacency list stores only present edges and uses less space for a sparse graph.
Breadth first search
Explain why BFS finds shortest paths by edge count in an unweighted graph.
It explores all vertices at distance d before any vertex at distance d+1.
Depth first search
Name one task for which DFS is a natural graph traversal.
DFS supports reachability, cycle detection, and topological ordering through finish times.
Cycle detection
Describe how a directed DFS detects a back edge.
An edge to a vertex currently on the recursion stack indicates a directed cycle.
Dijkstra condition
State the edge-weight condition required by Dijkstra's algorithm.
All edge weights must be nonnegative so finalized shortest distances cannot later decrease.
topics.title: Graphs

topics.description: Analyze asymptotic behavior and choose practical algorithmic trade-offs.
exercises: Big O meaning
Explain what O(n log n) says about an algorithm as input grows.
It gives an asymptotic upper growth bound up to constant factors for sufficiently large n.
Space trade-off
Give a case where using extra memory is a good algorithmic trade-off.
Caching repeated computations can reduce runtime when the memory budget permits it.
Lower bound
Explain why reading every input value imposes a linear lower bound.
An algorithm cannot determine a property dependent on an unread value.
Worst versus average
Distinguish worst-case from average-case complexity.
Worst-case bounds the most expensive input; average-case depends on a stated input distribution.
Algorithm selection
Select an algorithm when latency matters more than memory use.
Prefer the faster asymptotic or measured method when its extra memory remains within the available budget.
topics.title: Complexity and design

topics.description: Use executable examples, properties, and review to establish behavior.
exercises: Unit boundary
Design a unit test for a function that rejects negative quantities.
Call it with a negative value and assert the documented error without external dependencies.
Property test
Give a property that every list reversal implementation should satisfy.
Reversing twice yields the original list and preserves its length and elements.
Integration boundary
Explain what an integration test should cover for a repository adapter.
Exercise the adapter against a real or controlled persistence boundary and verify mapping and error behavior.
Regression test
Describe a regression test for an off-by-one loop bug.
Capture the smallest failing boundary input and assert the corrected result.
Test isolation
Explain why tests that share mutable global state become order dependent.
One test can alter what another observes, so failures vary with execution order.
topics.title: Testing and correctness

topics.description: Apply modular design, compatibility, and delivery practices.
exercises: Interface segregation
Explain how a broad interface can force clients to depend on unused operations.
Splitting role-specific interfaces lets each client depend only on operations it needs.
Merge conflict
Describe a safe workflow for resolving a conflicting change.
Understand both intents, edit the combined result, run relevant checks, and review the resolved diff.
Continuous delivery
Distinguish continuous delivery from continuous deployment.
Delivery keeps every change releasable; deployment automatically releases every passing change.
API compatibility
Evaluate whether removing a required response field is breaking.
Existing consumers may depend on the field, so removal changes the response contract.
Dependency direction
Explain why domain code should avoid depending directly on infrastructure details.
Keeping the dependency inward makes policy testable and infrastructure replaceable.
topics.title: Software design

topics.description: Reason about reliable networked services and their failure modes.
exercises: HTTP method choice
Choose an HTTP method for replacing a known resource.
PUT expresses replacement at a known URI and is idempotent.
Idempotent retry
Design an idempotency-key strategy for a retried request.
Persist the key with the first result and return that result for duplicate requests.
Eventual consistency
Give a user-visible consequence of eventual consistency.
Two replicas may temporarily return different values after a write.
TCP reliability
Name two mechanisms TCP uses for reliable ordered delivery.
Sequence numbers order bytes; acknowledgements and retransmission recover loss.
Timeout handling
Explain why a client timeout does not prove a server operation was not applied.
The response can be delayed or lost after the server commits, so retries need idempotent semantics.
topics.title: Web and distributed systems
